analysis.one_liner: Blocks the Interior Department from protecting Grand Canyon-area federal land from new uranium mining claims.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced, heard once in a House subcommittee, and never received a vote in the House before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2011 the Interior Department was moving to pull about one million acres of federal land in northern Arizona out of new uranium mining claims, because of concerns that mining could contaminate the groundwater feeding the Grand Canyon. This bill would have stopped the government from finalizing or extending that withdrawal unless Congress passed a law explicitly approving it, and would have made the withdrawal legally void. The bill never made it out of the House Natural Resources Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Uranium mining companies would benefit most: the bill would keep roughly one million acres of the Arizona Strip open to new mining claims, protecting access to what the bill's own findings call an estimated 375 million pounds of high-grade uranium ore. Some local officials and workers would also gain from potential mining jobs and tax revenue the bill's findings predict.

how_it_helps.text: The bill forbids the Interior Secretary from extending, renewing, or issuing the withdrawal described in Public Land Order 7773 unless Congress passes a law that explicitly refers to this Act, and voids any such withdrawal notice. [S2] [S3]

It would keep open to new mining claims about one million acres of federal and National Forest land in Coconino and Mohave Counties, Arizona, near the Grand Canyon, preserving access to a large uranium deposit. [S3]
The bill's findings argue the mining is low-impact underground 'breccia pipe' mining that would create permanent, well-paying jobs and revenue for federal, state, and local governments. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental risk: the land sits in the Grand Canyon watershed, and the withdrawal was proposed specifically over concerns that uranium mining could contaminate groundwater. The bill would remove the executive branch's main tool for shielding that watershed, and any contamination of a regional aquifer could be impossible to reverse.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public near the Grand Canyon

drawbacks.text: Mining supporters argued the withdrawal locks up a major domestic uranium resource that could create jobs and government revenue, and cited a February 2011 draft environmental review that found no conclusive evidence the modern mining had contaminated groundwater in the regional aquifer. [S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill reaches far beyond a compromise: it doesn't just weigh mining against conservation, it strips the Interior Department of the power to withdraw the land at all without a future act of Congress, even if new evidence of harm emerged. [S3]

Critics of uranium mining near the Canyon have long noted that once groundwater in a regional aquifer is contaminated, it cannot be cleaned up — a risk that science on breccia pipe mining has not fully resolved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real economic upside — jobs and revenue from a large uranium deposit — but its central effect was to bar the Interior Department from protecting roughly a million acres of the Grand Canyon watershed from new mining claims, not just for a review period but unless Congress affirmatively stepped in. Given the uncertainty around groundwater contamination from this type of mining and the difficulty of reversing it, the cost to the public outweighed the benefit, which is presumably why it drew no support beyond a dozen House Republicans and never reached a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittees, got one hearing on November 3, 2011, and was never brought to a markup or a House vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Trent Franks introduced the bill on October 12, 2011, with ten other Republican cosponsors joining. [S1] [S3] [S4]

The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources; on October 17 it was sent to the Subcommittees on National Parks, Forests and Public Lands and on Energy and Mineral Resources. [S5]
A subcommittee hearing was held on November 3, 2011 — the only action after referral. [S5]
No further action was taken: the bill never reached a committee markup or a floor vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S5]

The bill targeted Public Land Order 7773, the June 2011 withdrawal of roughly one million acres from new mining claims in northern Arizona over concerns about impacts to the Grand Canyon watershed. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Protection of the Grand Canyon watershed came out ahead: because the bill died, the Interior Department's withdrawal of the land from new mining claims was never undone, and in January 2012 the department finalized a 20-year withdrawal of the area. Uranium mining companies seeking new claims on the Arizona Strip came out worse off than they would have under the bill.

for.name: Trent Franks
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to block the Interior Department's uranium mining withdrawal.

for.name: Uranium mining interests on the Arizona Strip
for.role: Mining claim holders and the uranium industry
for.what_they_did: Pushed to keep the northern Arizona lands open to new uranium mining claims after the Interior Department proposed the withdrawal.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees, held one hearing, and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the House floor. [S5]

against.name: Ken Salazar
against.what_they_did: Finalized a 20-year withdrawal of about one million acres from new uranium mining claims in January 2012, making the bill's target policy a reality and the bill largely moot.

against.name: Environmental and conservation groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly supported the withdrawal and opposed opening the Grand Canyon watershed to new uranium mining.

sides.party_line_note: All twelve sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and no vote ever occurred, so the record shows no Democratic support and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have kept about a million acres of the Arizona Strip open to new mining claims, protecting access to a large high-grade uranium deposit. The land sits in the Grand Canyon watershed, so the industry's gain came at the public's expense in environmental risk to the region's groundwater.

industries.industry: Northern Arizona tourism and communities near the Grand Canyon
industries.note: The bill would have weakened the withdrawal that was proposed specifically to protect the Grand Canyon watershed, where the region's economy and public water resources depend on clean groundwater. This industry's interest in the bill ran alongside the public's, since the bill threatened the resource both rely on.
